title: Deployment Options
description: Explore the main deployment options for ASP.NET Core applications. Compare self-hosting with Kestrel, IIS on Windows, Nginx reverse proxy on Linux, and cloud platforms like Azure App Service. Learn the publish command and how to choose the right deployment target.

blocks.text: Deployment is the process of moving your application from a development machine to a production environment where real users can access it. ASP.NET Core is cross-platform and runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS, giving you many hosting options. The right choice depends on your team's expertise, your budget, your scaling requirements, and your existing infrastructure.

Before deployment, you must publish your application. Publishing compiles your code, resolves dependencies, and produces a self-contained folder or single-file executable that can run on the target machine without the .NET SDK installed.

The dotnet publish command is the standard way to prepare an ASP.NET Core application for deployment. It produces a deployable output in a specified folder. You can publish as a framework-dependent deployment (smaller, requires .NET runtime on the server) or a self-contained deployment (larger, includes the runtime, runs anywhere).

blocks.title: Publishing an ASP.NET Core Application
blocks.content: The dotnet publish command with common flags for production-ready output.
blocks.code:
# Framework-dependent deployment (smaller output, needs .NET runtime on server)
dotnet publish MyApp.csproj \
  --configuration Release \
  --output ./publish \
  --no-restore

# Self-contained deployment for Linux x64 (larger output, no runtime needed)
dotnet publish MyApp.csproj \
  --configuration Release \
  --output ./publish \
  --self-contained true \
  --runtime linux-x64 \
  -p:PublishSingleFile=true \
  -p:IncludeNativeLibrariesForSelfExtract=true

blocks.title: Framework-Dependent vs Self-Contained
blocks.text: Framework-dependent deployments are smaller and let you update the .NET runtime independently. Self-contained deployments include the runtime, are larger, and work even if the target machine has no .NET installed. Choose framework-dependent for cloud VMs where you control the runtime, and self-contained for environments where you cannot guarantee runtime availability.

Kestrel is the cross-platform web server included with ASP.NET Core. It is fast, lightweight, and designed to handle production traffic. In many deployment scenarios — especially Linux containers — Kestrel is the only web server you need. It can serve directly on ports 80 and 443, though in production it is common to place a reverse proxy in front of it.

Kestrel has configurable limits for request body size, connection limits, and request timeouts. These limits protect your application from resource exhaustion attacks. In Program.cs, you can configure Kestrel directly using the WebHost or Generic Host configuration APIs.

blocks.text: Internet Information Services (IIS) is the traditional Windows web server. ASP.NET Core runs behind IIS using the ASP.NET Core Hosting Bundle, which installs the .NET runtime and the ANCM (ASP.NET Core Module) — a native IIS module that forwards requests to Kestrel. IIS handles process management, Windows authentication, and SSL termination.

blocks.title: IIS Deployment Considerations
items: Install the ASP.NET Core Hosting Bundle on the target server before deploying
Publish your app to a folder and configure the IIS website to point at it
IIS manages the Kestrel process and restarts it if it crashes (OutOfProcess hosting)
Web.config is generated during publish and tells ANCM how to start your application
Best for organizations with existing Windows infrastructure and IIS expertise

blocks.text: Nginx as a Reverse Proxy on Linux

On Linux, Nginx is the most common reverse proxy for ASP.NET Core. Nginx listens on ports 80 and 443, handles SSL termination, and forwards requests to Kestrel running on a local port like 5000. This architecture is standard for Linux deployments and gives you battle-tested TLS configuration, static file serving, and load balancing.

blocks.text: Azure App Service, AWS Elastic Beanstalk, and Google Cloud Run all provide managed hosting for ASP.NET Core. You push your code or Docker image, and the platform handles the infrastructure — scaling, SSL, load balancing, and deployment slots. This is the fastest path to production if you do not want to manage servers.

blocks.title: Cloud Deployment Options at a Glance
items: Azure App Service: Managed PaaS for .NET apps with built-in scaling, slots, and monitoring. Publish directly from Visual Studio or GitHub Actions.
AWS Elastic Beanstalk: Managed EC2-based hosting with auto-scaling groups. Upload a ZIP or Docker image and AWS manages the rest.
Azure Container Apps / AWS ECS / Google Cloud Run: Container-based serverless platforms. Ideal if your app is already containerized with Docker.
VPS (DigitalOcean, Linode, Vultr): Simple virtual machines where you manage the server yourself. Cheapest option but requires DevOps knowledge.

terms.definition: ASP.NET Core's built-in cross-platform web server, capable of serving production traffic directly.
The CLI command that compiles and packages an application for deployment to a target environment.
A server (Nginx, IIS, Apache) that sits in front of your application, handling SSL, routing, and load balancing.
A publish output that includes the .NET runtime, enabling the app to run on machines without .NET installed.
A publish output that relies on the .NET runtime being installed on the target machine, resulting in a smaller deployment.

blocks.title: Start with Kestrel + Nginx
blocks.text: For most new projects, deploying Kestrel behind Nginx on a Linux VPS or cloud VM is the simplest, most cost-effective starting point. You can migrate to a managed platform like Azure App Service later without rewriting your application.

blocks.title: Lesson Summary: Deployment Options
points: dotnet publish produces a deployable output — choose framework-dependent or self-contained based on your target
Kestrel is the built-in, cross-platform web server capable of production workloads
IIS on Windows uses ANCM to forward requests to Kestrel, managing process lifetime and SSL
Nginx on Linux acts as a reverse proxy, handling SSL termination and forwarding to Kestrel on a local port
Cloud platforms (Azure, AWS, GCP) handle infrastructure management at the cost of platform lock-in
Choose your deployment target based on existing infrastructure, team expertise, and scaling needs
blocks.takeaway: ASP.NET Core gives you flexibility in where and how you deploy. Start simple — Kestrel on Linux with Nginx is a solid production setup that costs little and scales well. Move to managed cloud platforms when you need features like auto-scaling, staging slots, or integrated monitoring.

blocks.title: Exercise: Publish and Prepare for Deployment
blocks.description: Publish an ASP.NET Core application and prepare it for deployment to a Linux server with Nginx.
steps: Run dotnet publish with --configuration Release and --output ./publish to create a deployment folder
Examine the published output — identify the executable, web.config, and dll files
Run the published application directly with dotnet MyApp.dll and confirm it starts on port 5000
Write an Nginx server block configuration that listens on port 80 and proxies to localhost:5000
Test the Nginx configuration with nginx -t and explain what the proxy_set_header directives do
Describe the steps needed to deploy this to a real Linux server (SSH, file transfer, process manager)
blocks.expectedOutcome: A published application that runs locally, an Nginx configuration ready for production, and a clear understanding of the deployment workflow from development to a Linux server.

items.text: I can run dotnet publish and explain what it produces
items.hint: dotnet publish compiles and packages your app. Use --self-contained for no-runtime targets.

items.text: I understand the difference between framework-dependent and self-contained deployments
items.hint: Framework-dependent is smaller. Self-contained includes the runtime and works anywhere.

items.text: I can describe Kestrel's role and when it needs a reverse proxy
items.hint: Kestrel serves HTTP. A reverse proxy (Nginx/IIS) in front handles SSL, static files, and load balancing.

items.text: I know how IIS works with ASP.NET Core through ANCM
items.hint: ANCM forwards IIS requests to Kestrel. IIS handles process lifetime, auth, and SSL.

items.text: I can explain the trade-offs between a VPS and a managed cloud platform
items.hint: VPS is cheaper but you manage everything. Cloud platforms handle ops but cost more and add lock-in.
